title: Refuge of the bad
hookLine: the Tao is the treasure of the good and the refuge of the bad (Tao Te Ching 62)

lines: A CHAIR, A PLATE, NO SPEECH.
cards: Who gets to come back after they've failed? Some households answer with a chair at the kitchen table. The cousin who lost the job.
The friend who said the unforgivable thing at the wedding. The kid who got suspended. Nobody gives a speech first; somebody puts down a plate.
Chapter sixty-two of the Tao Te Ching says the Way itself works like that table. It belongs to the good, and it also shelters the ones who aren't.

teach.b: First, one place for two kinds of people. The chapter calls the Tao the treasure of the good and, in the same breath, what the not-good hold on to for protection.
The good treasure it; the ones who've gone wrong hide in it. Same Way. Second, a question.
Even if people are not good, the chapter asks, more or less, why should they be thrown away? It doesn't answer with a rule. The question does the work.

The chapter pictures a ruler being crowned, officials appointed, grand presents brought in: a disc of precious jade, a fine team of horses. Better than all of it, it says, would be to sit still and offer this Way.
The most valuable thing in the room isn't on a cart. Fourth, why the ancients prized it.
The chapter recalls a saying: through the Tao, those who seek will find, and those who have done wrong will escape it. That's the refuge.
Not a hiding place from consequences, exactly, but a place where a person who failed isn't finished.

That might be the coworker who blew the deadline, the friend who flaked, or the person in the mirror who did the thing again. The chapter's question follows them all into the room. Why throw anyone away?

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty-two as a teaching that no one is beyond the Way: they keep the door open to people who have failed instead of writing them off.

games.q: what does “refuge of the bad” mean?
o: the Way as a shelter even for those who've gone wrong
a punishment the Tao saves for those who do harm
a prison where wrongdoers are kept from good people

p: hold on to it for protection

s: chapter sixty-two says the Tao belongs only to good people
it calls the Tao the treasure of the good and the refuge of the not-good.
the chapter asks why people who aren't good should be thrown away
it leaves the question standing instead of answering with a rule.
the chapter says precious jade is the best gift for a new ruler
it says sitting still and offering the Way would be better than jade and horses.

games.q: a ruler is being crowned, and you can bring one gift. what does chapter sixty-two say is worth most?
o: sitting still and offering the Way.
games.why: the chapter says that better than jade and horses would be to sit still and offer this Way.

practice: Bring to mind one person who has messed up lately; it might be someone close, or it might be you. You don't have to excuse what happened: just picture pulling out a chair and setting down a plate, with no speech.
If that's hard, let it be hard, and keep the chair there anyway.
